paragraph: The Approximate Nearest Neighbor (ANN) search problem involves retrieving the 𝑘closest points to a given query point 𝑞in a𝑑- dimensional metric space. This problem is foundational in database systems, machine learning, information retrieval, and computer vision, and has seen growing importance in large language models (LLMs) [ 34], particularly in retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) pipelines, where relevant documents must be retrieved efficiently from large corpora [ 18,39]. More generally, any vector database system implements some form of ANN search to enable efficient vector similarity queries [ 4,24,55]. For a comprehensive overview of additional applications, we refer the reader to the following surveys [40, 42, 63]. Several classes of algorithms have been developed for ANN. Hash-based approaches (e.g., Locality-Sensitive Hashing [ 11,26, Conference’17, Washington, DC, USA 2026. ACM ISBN 978-x-xxxx-xxxx-x/YYYY/MM https://doi.org/10.1145/nnnnnnn.nnnnnnn29]) offer theoretical guarantees on retrieval quality but often strug- gle in practical settings [ 57]. Quantization-based methods cluster data and search among representative centroids, yielding speedups at the cost of approximation error [ 21,32,54]. Graph-based ap- proaches [ 31,46,63], particularly hierarchical variants [ 43,46,49], have gained attention due to their strong empirical performance and scalability. These methods build graphs over the dataset and perform greedy traversal to locate approximate neighbors quickly.1 Among them, the Hierarchical Navigable Small World (HNSW) [ 46] graph is widely used in practice [ 8,16,17,48,56,62]. HNSW or- ganizes data into multiple layers by assigning each point to a ran- domly chosen level and constructs navigable small-world graphs at each layer. While HNSW is widely used in many existing tools and is easy to implement, it lacks formal guarantees on query time, while the upper-bound on its worst-case complexity is linear to dataset size inadversarial settings [ 30,58]. In contrast, earlier theo- retically grounded hierarchical structures like Cover Trees [ 6,36], provide logarithmic query time guarantees by constructing hierar- chies using𝑟-nets.2However, these structures are relatively difficult to implement and often do not scale well to real datasets, limiting their practical adoption. In this work, we introduce a general class of hierarchical graphs for ANN search, grounded in 𝜀-net theory from computational ge- ometry [ 28]. In these graphs, each layer forms an 𝜀-net of the preced- ing one, while the choice of proximity graph at each layer remains agnostic, allowing the use of any suitable graph. The framework is general enough to include a wide range of graph-based ANN algo- rithms introduced in the recent literature [ 19,31,32,47,55,59,63]; therefore, we treat such graphs abstractly and focus on their prop- erties. Our framework establishes time guarantees for such indices as a function of the properties of the underlying proximity graph. Notably, we show that HNSW is a special case of HENN with high probability, corresponding to the choice of NSW as the base proximity graph. As a crucial building block, we further propose budget-aware practical algorithms for computing 𝜀-nets on large datasets, enabling the scalable construction of these hierarchical graphs and offering a mechanism for compressing these indices by trading additional preprocessing time for improved space efficiency. Our contributions can be summarized as follows: •We introduce a general property for hierarchical indices in ANN search, called Hierarchical 𝜀-Net Navigation (HENN) , where each layer is an𝜀-net of the preceding one. This framework is agnostic to the choice of proximity graph and can be combined with 1Related work is further discussed in Appendix 9. 2Here,𝑟-nets differ from 𝜀-nets as defined in computational geometry. By 𝑟-net, we refer to a subset of points that ensures every point in the space is within distance 𝑟of some net point. In contrast, 𝜀-nets refer to subsets that intersect all "heavy" ranges, containing more than an 𝜀fraction of the total volume or weight. (left). Layers are numbered bottom-up, with layer 0being the point set 𝑋and the last layer (layer 𝐿) called the root. common graphs such as kNN, NSW [ 46], NSG [ 19], RNG [ 59], or other existing ANN graphs [63]. •We formalize a property of proximity graphs, called the recall bound , which quantifies how well a graph performs when used within a hierarchical index. •We establish probabilistic query-time bounds for HENN graphs, which are logarithmic in the dataset size and parameterized by the properties of the underlying proximity graph. •We show that HNSW is a HENN with high probability, when NSW is used as the proximity graph, thereby yielding formal probabilistic time guarantees for HNSW . •A key component in building HENN graphs is computing 𝜀-nets. Existing randomized algorithms [ 28] provide𝜀-nets only with a fixed success probability, while deterministic methods based on discrepancy theory [ 9] are impractical in high dimensions. We design a budget-aware algorithm that allows the user to specify a preprocessing budget. More preprocessing time increases the probability of successfully constructing an 𝜀-net. •Our budget-aware algorithm leads to the construction of more compact indexes , effectively yielding a compressed version of HNSW while preserving recall. Our empirical evaluation confirms the theoretical time bounds forHENN andHNSW as a special case of HENN, as well as for other HENN-based structures. We show that these bounds hold with high probability (greater than 0.99) in practical scenarios, and further demonstrate the flexibility of HENN by integrating it with different proximity graphs and comparing their performance. In addition, we illustrate how our budget-aware algorithm enables the construction of compressed indices: by allocating more preprocessing time, one can reduce index size while maintaining recall, highlighting a clear tradeoff between preprocessing cost and query performance. Finally, we implement HENN as a new index in the popular Faiss [ 17] library and compare it against state-of-the-art baselines, showing its equivalence to HNSW and empirically validating our theoretical claims.

Given a point set 𝑋, a proximity graph is a graph whose vertices correspond to the points in 𝑋, and whose edges connect pairs of points according to a proximity criterion in the underlying space. The goal is to preserve the neighborhood structure of the data so that ANN queries can be answered by navigating the graph. A more detailed discussion of these graph types is provided in Appendix A. 𝜀-net Hierarchy . Each layerL𝑖in a HENN graph is an 𝜀-net, with a choice of𝜀that results in the optimum query time (Equation 1). This𝜀-net is defined on the range space (𝑋,R), where𝑋denotes the input point set and Ris the family of ring ranges defined below. Definition 2 (Ring Ranges). Given a set of points 𝑋, and a distance function d, aring𝑅∈ R is specified with a base point 𝑝∈R𝑑and two values 𝑟1<𝑟2. Any point in 𝑋with distance within two values𝑟1and𝑟2from𝑝falls inside the ring. Formally, 𝑅∩𝑋={𝑥∈𝑋|𝑟1≤d(𝑥,𝑝)≤𝑟2} Proposition 2. The VC-dimension of the ring range space, (𝑋,R), isΘ(𝑑). The correctness of Proposition 2 follows the fact that each ring range𝑅:⟨𝑝,𝑟1,𝑟2⟩can be formulated by mixing the two ball ranges 𝑅′:d(𝑥,𝑝)≤𝑟2and𝑅′′:d(𝑥,𝑝)≤𝑟1as𝑅=𝑅′−𝑅′′. Hence, due to the mixing property of range spaces [ 25], the VC-dim of the ring ranges is two times the VC-dim of the distance ranges, i.e., Θ(𝑑). Recall that we require the distance dto satisfy a VC-dim of Θ(𝑑) for balls. Following Proposition 2 and Theorem 1, one can find an 𝜀-net of size𝑚𝜀=𝑂(𝑑 𝜀log1 𝜀), for the ring range space, for a given value 𝜀. The construction details of 𝜀-net are provided in Section 6. Hereafter, whenever we refer to an 𝜀-net of a point set, we mean an 𝜀-net with respect to the range space of rings defined on that point set. The Value of 𝜀.To satisfy the HENN property, each layer L𝑖+1 must form an 𝜀-net of the preceding layer L𝑖. We define a function E:N→(0,1)that specifies the value of 𝜀for a layer of size 𝑛. In other words,L𝑖+1is anE(|L𝑖|)-net ofL𝑖. For the graph to be HENN, the required value of 𝜀is 𝜀=E(|L𝑖|)=E(𝑛)=Θ(︂𝑑log𝑛 𝑛)︂ , (1) where𝑛=|L𝑖|. In the next section, we show that this choice of 𝜀leads to optimal query time guarantees on the graph.

Query Answering Using a HENN Graph . During the query time, given a query point 𝑞∈R𝑑, the goal is to find the approximate nearest neighbor of 𝑞within𝑋. Building on this connection, we derive probabilistic time guarantees for HNSW. We begin with a simplified description of HNSW [ 46]. During preprocessing, points are inserted incrementally into the index. For each new point, a random variable determines its maximum layer, with the probability of assignment to higher layers decreasing ex- ponentially. After the layers are determined, the point is connected at each layer to its nearest neighbors among the previously inserted points, identified using the greedy search procedure (Algorithm 1). Equivalently, HNSW can be viewed as starting from a base layer containing all points and recursively constructing higher layers by randomly sampling subsets of points, such that the size of each layer decreases exponentially with the level. Comparison. The randomized algorithm is straightforward to implement, requiring only random sampling from each layer L𝑖 to construct the subsequent layer L𝑖+1. However, it is inherently randomized and provides running-time guarantees in expectation. Furthermore, its time complexity depends on the time to verify if the selected set is indeed an 𝜀-net. In contrast, the deterministic discrepancy-based algorithm de- terministically constructs an 𝜀-net by progressively halving each layerL𝑖. This process involves only halving L𝑖a couple of times to identify the next layer L𝑖+1(See BuildEpsNetDisc in Algorithm 5). Nevertheless, the running time of the discrepancy-based algorithm depends exponentially on the dimensionality of the input points, which makes it impractical. 6.2 Budget-Aware Algorithm for Constructing 𝜀-nets To bridge the gap between sampling-based methods (fast but prob- abilistic) and discrepancy-based methods (deterministic but compu- tationally expensive), we introduce a budget-aware algorithm . This approach allows the user to control a resource budget, thereby ad- justing the trade-off between construction speed and the probability that the resulting set forms a valid 𝜀-net. Given a user-specified timing budget B, which determines the allowed construction time, we design an algorithm that achieves success with a probability depending on B. This approach is in- spired by the deterministic 𝜀-net construction via finding an unhit range, known as Net-Finder algorithm [ 51]. Our proposed Budget- Aware algorithm is presented in Algorithm 3.

One advantage of the Budget-Aware al- gorithm is its ability to compress HENN index and, consequently, HNSW index. Experiments Setup . We use standard benchmark datasets for ANN search [ 3], including SIFT-128 [33],GIST-960 [33],Fashion-MNIST- 784[65], and NYTimes-256 [52], along with synthetic datasets (uni- form distributions and mixtures of Gaussians). Both Euclidean ( ℓ2- norm) and cosine (angular) distance metrics are considered. For proximity graphs, we evaluate several structures, including KNN , KGraph [15],11NSW [47],NSG [19], and FAANG [27]. Our meth- ods are denoted as HENN +X, where𝑋specifies the underlying proximity graph used in the construction. Additional details on experimental setup can be found at the Appendix E.1.

Verification of Time Guarantees . We study the impact of several parameters on query time. Figure 4 illustrates the effect of dataset size𝑛on query time. For each dataset, we subsampled 𝑛points and generated random queries within the space. Across all datasets, the query time grows logarithmically with 𝑛, consistent with Theorem 4. 11Here, KGraph refers to NN-descent applied on a 𝑘NN graph, following [15].Similarly, Figure 16 (in Appendix E.4) reports the number of visited hops during greedy search with a similar trend. Similar experiments on more datasets is provided in Appendix E.4. The effect of the proximity graph degree is shown in Figure 5, where we varied the degree across all layers. The results indicate that query time scales linearly with the graph degree 𝜋. Figure 6 examines the effect of data dimensionality 𝑑on query time. Starting from𝑑=2, as𝑑increases, the search is more likely to get trapped in local minima (curse of dimensionality), which accelerates query by halting the greedy search early. However, once 𝑑exceeds 64, the query time becomes dominated by the linear dependence on 𝑑. Similar results on the number of visited hops and other datasets are in Appendix E.

Recall Bound of Popular Proximity Graphs . In our experiments, we empirically estimate the recall bound (i.e., the inverse CDF) ofa proximity graph by sampling and fitting an appropriate density function. Deriving a closed-form expression for the recall bound, or a closed-form characterization of the rank distribution, remains an interesting direction for future work. Focusing on specific input data distributionsD(see Section 4.1) may further facilitate such analyses. Doing so could enable an end-to-end closed-form characterization of the query-time distribution of HENN, as well as of flat indices constructed via 𝜀-nets. 9 Related Work In this section, we review the literature most relevant to our work. Hierarchical Methods for ANN. A notable class of approaches for solving the ANN problem is based on hierarchical structures. One of the most widely used methods in this category is Hierarchical Navigable Small World ( HNSW ) [46], which constructs a multi- layered structure of navigable small-world graphs to enable efficient search. Interestingly, the core idea of hierarchical organization can be traced back to earlier work in computational geometry, including Cover Trees [6] and Navigating Nets [36]. Hierarchical Navigable Small World (HNSW) graphs [ 46] con- struct a multi-layered hierarchy of navigable small world (NSW) graphs. An NSW graph serves as an efficient approximation of the Delaunay graph [ 25], which is known to be an optimal structure for solving the approximate nearest neighbor (ANN) problem [ 47]. The Delaunay graph is closely related to the Voronoi diagram, which partitions the space into cells based on their proximity to the points in the dataset. Unlike the Delaunay graph, which requires explicit geometric computation, NSW graphs are built incrementally by inserting points and connecting them to their approximate nearest neighbors [ 47]. During insertion and querying, HNSW employs a greedy search algorithm (Algorithm 1) to navigate through the graph and locate nearby points. To improve scalability, HNSW orga- nizes the data in a hierarchy where the number of nodes decreases exponentially across layers, resulting in 𝑂(log𝑛)layers and a total space complexity of 𝑂(𝑛). The Cover Tree [ 6] and Navigating Nets [ 36] are hierarchical data structures for nearest neighbor search in general metric spaces. Both achieve logarithmic query times by recursively organizing data into nested layers, cover trees through covering and separa- tion invariants, and navigating nets via sequences of 𝑟-nets that approximate the dataset at multiple scales. While they offer strong theoretical guarantees and predictable performance, these methods are challenging to implement and scale poorly in practice, limiting their adoption in modern large-scale applications. Beyond HNSW, several other hierarchical indices and heuris- tics have been proposed. None being generalized to HENN. For example, HVS organizes data into coarse Voronoi regions that are refined hierarchically, enabling layered navigation and accelerating search by progressively narrowing the candidate set [ 43]. HCNNG instead builds multiple hierarchical clusterings and merges them into a proximity graph, leveraging both global and local structure. By combining clustering with MST-based connectivity, HCNNG re- duces construction overhead while maintaining competitive query performance [49]. Some methods integrate hierarchical tree structures with graph refinement, while large-scale libraries such as FAISS [ 35] adopt hierarchical inverted file strategies. In FAISS, coarse quantization partitions the dataset into clusters, which are then refined with product quantization (PQ) [32].

Other Solutions for ANN. Solutions to the nearest neighbor prob- lem can be categorized along several dimensions. One common dis- tinction is between classical methods, which primarily target the ex- act NN problem. Examples include k-d trees [ 5], ball trees [ 53], and Delaunay triangulations [ 26]. While effective in low-dimensional spaces, these methods typically fail to scale in high-dimensional settings. Another broad category includes quantization-based meth- ods [ 21,32,54], which cluster the data and represent points by theirassigned centroids (codewords), thereby approximating distances efficiently. Additionally, hashing-based methods such as Locality- Sensitive Hashing (LSH [ 11]) provide theoretical guarantees and have been widely used for high-dimensional ANN, and finally, the graph-based methods [ 43,46,47,58]. For comprehensive overviews of these and other approaches, we refer the reader to the following surveys [ 4,24,40,42,55,63]. Beyond graph topology, several lines of work improve ANN accuracy and efficiency through quantiza- tion. Guo, et al. [ 23] introduce direction-sensitive quantizers that better preserve angular similarity, enabling faster high-dimensional inference with competitive recall. Similarly, Rabitq [ 20] provides a quantization scheme with theoretical reconstruction-error guar- antees designed specifically for ANN search, showing that quanti- zation can substantially reduce memory while retaining accuracy. These works mainly focus on compressing the data vectors used for distance estimation, whereas our focus is on the structure and navigability of the search graph itself. Another complementary line is probabilistic search guidance [ 44], which proposes stochastic transition rules to escape local minima and improve robustness of greedy search. Such methods modify the search dynamics rather than the graph structure. The above systems are orthogonal and compatible with our theoretical contributions. Quantization-based methods can be applied inside any graph index to reduce vector memory footprint. Similarly, probabilistic routing modifies how the search moves on a fixed graph.

Worst-Case Performance Analysis. Several works study the lim- itations of graph-based ANN indices. Indyk et al. [ 30] show that HNSW can require linear query time on adversarial datasets. Wang et al. [ 64] propose Steiner-hardness as a graph-native measure of query difficulty, capturing structural factors that influence cost and enabling the design of unbiased workloads. While these ap- proaches characterize hard queries or highlight specific failure cases on proximity graphs , our analysis takes a complementary view by providing general bounds on query time for HENN as a function of the underlying proximity graph. Moreover, empirical results sug- gest that the worst-case recall bounds rarely manifest in practice, as they remain stable across real-world datasets.

[ 64] propose Steiner-hardness as a graph-native measure of query difficulty, capturing structural factors that influence cost and enabling the design of unbiased workloads. Comparison with Other Structural Analysis. Other recent works focus on improving or analyzing proximity graph constructions. Yang et al. [ 66] revisit construction strategies for indices like RNG and NSWG, optimizing pruning and edge selection to reduce build time without harming query performance. Diwan et al. [ 14] study the fundamental limits of navigable graphs, proving upper and lower bounds on node degree for efficient greedy routing. In con- trast, our contribution is structural: we introduce HENN as a graph- agnostic framework based on 𝜀-net layering, yielding provable polylogarithmic query-time guarantees for any underlying prox- imity graph. DiskANN [ 31] shows that a navigable graph com- bined with SSD-aware prefetching enables billion-scale search with near–HNSW accuracy. Lin & Zhao [ 41] provide a critical examina- tion of proximity-graph search, showing that well-constructed flat graphs can perform competitively and highlighting when greedy search succeeds or fails. Practical engineering optimizations also matter: Coleman et al. [ 10] demonstrate that simple node reordering can substantially reduce cache misses and latency. Most recently, Munyampirwa et al. [ 50] show that the performance of HNSW largely comes from a set of high-degree “hub” nodes, and that flattening the hierarchy yields similar recall and speed. 10 Conclusion We introduced HENN , a structural property for hierarchical graph- based indices in ANN search that unifies theoretical guarantees with practical efficiency. By organizing layers as 𝜀-nets, HENN achieves provable polylogarithmic query time while retaining a simple and implementable design. We further provided a probabilistic analysis ofHNSW , shedding light on the reasons behind its strong empirical performance. To support practical adoption, we developed a budget- aware algorithm for 𝜀-net construction, allowing practitioners to balance preprocessing time against recall quality.

𝜀-nets To bridge the gap between sampling-based methods (fast but prob- abilistic) and discrepancy-based methods (deterministic but compu- tationally expensive), we introduce a budget-aware algorithm . This approach allows the user to control a resource budget, thereby ad- justing the trade-off between construction speed and the probability that the resulting set forms a valid 𝜀-net. Given a user-specified timing budget B, which determines the allowed construction time, we design an algorithm that achieves success with a probability depending on B. This approach is in- spired by the deterministic 𝜀-net construction via finding an unhit range, known as Net-Finder algorithm [ 51]. Our proposed Budget- Aware algorithm is presented in Algorithm 3.

In this section, we empirically validate the theoretical results of the proposed HENN structure and assess the algorithms developed for its construction. Furthermore, we implement the general HENN graph within the widely used Faiss library [ 17,35], providing it as a new index alongside the existing popular ANN indices. The code is publicly available at this anonymous repository. Additional experi- mental results are provided in Appendix E due to space constraints. We organize the experiments into the following parts: (1)Experiments Setup. Description of datasets (both real and syn- thetic), baseline methods, evaluation metrics, and configuration details. (2)Proximity Graph Integration. Integration of different prox- imity graphs into the HENN framework and evaluation of their performance. (3)Verification of Time Guarantees. Empirical validation of the time bounds proved in Section 4. (4)𝜀-net Construction. Comparison of introduced algorithms for building𝜀-nets (Section 6) and their impact when integrated into HENN. (5)Comparison with Other ANN Indices. Evaluation of a stan- dard implementation of HENN integrated with the HNSW index in the widely used FAISS library, and comparison against other indices available there, including LSH [ 11], IVF-PQ [ 32], and NSG [19]. (6)More on Recall Bound. Comparison of different proximity graphs with different recall bounds and deriving the probability distribution over query time of HENN. 10This requires calculating all the distances to the randomly selected point 𝑝. Using optimized libraries for matrix multiplication, this step can be made faster (almost linear) in practice.

Verification of Time Guarantees . We study the impact of several parameters on query time. Figure 4 illustrates the effect of dataset size𝑛on query time. For each dataset, we subsampled 𝑛points and generated random queries within the space. Across all datasets, the query time grows logarithmically with 𝑛, consistent with Theorem 4. 11Here, KGraph refers to NN-descent applied on a 𝑘NN graph, following [15].Similarly, Figure 16 (in Appendix E.4) reports the number of visited hops during greedy search with a similar trend. Similar experiments on more datasets is provided in Appendix E.4. The effect of the proximity graph degree is shown in Figure 5, where we varied the degree across all layers. The results indicate that query time scales linearly with the graph degree 𝜋. Figure 6 examines the effect of data dimensionality 𝑑on query time. Starting from𝑑=2, as𝑑increases, the search is more likely to get trapped in local minima (curse of dimensionality), which accelerates query by halting the greedy search early. However, once 𝑑exceeds 64, the query time becomes dominated by the linear dependence on 𝑑. Similar results on the number of visited hops and other datasets are in Appendix E.

Hierarchical Methods for ANN. A notable class of approaches for solving the ANN problem is based on hierarchical structures. One of the most widely used methods in this category is Hierarchical Navigable Small World ( HNSW ) [46], which constructs a multi- layered structure of navigable small-world graphs to enable efficient search. Interestingly, the core idea of hierarchical organization can be traced back to earlier work in computational geometry, including Cover Trees [6] and Navigating Nets [36]. Hierarchical Navigable Small World (HNSW) graphs [ 46] con- struct a multi-layered hierarchy of navigable small world (NSW) graphs. An NSW graph serves as an efficient approximation of the Delaunay graph [ 25], which is known to be an optimal structure for solving the approximate nearest neighbor (ANN) problem [ 47]. The Delaunay graph is closely related to the Voronoi diagram, which partitions the space into cells based on their proximity to the points in the dataset. Unlike the Delaunay graph, which requires explicit geometric computation, NSW graphs are built incrementally by inserting points and connecting them to their approximate nearest neighbors [ 47]. During insertion and querying, HNSW employs a greedy search algorithm (Algorithm 1) to navigate through the graph and locate nearby points. To improve scalability, HNSW orga- nizes the data in a hierarchy where the number of nodes decreases exponentially across layers, resulting in 𝑂(log𝑛)layers and a total space complexity of 𝑂(𝑛). The Cover Tree [ 6] and Navigating Nets [ 36] are hierarchical data structures for nearest neighbor search in general metric spaces. Both achieve logarithmic query times by recursively organizing data into nested layers, cover trees through covering and separa- tion invariants, and navigating nets via sequences of 𝑟-nets that approximate the dataset at multiple scales. While they offer strong theoretical guarantees and predictable performance, these methods are challenging to implement and scale poorly in practice, limiting their adoption in modern large-scale applications. Beyond HNSW, several other hierarchical indices and heuris- tics have been proposed. None being generalized to HENN. For example, HVS organizes data into coarse Voronoi regions that are refined hierarchically, enabling layered navigation and accelerating search by progressively narrowing the candidate set [ 43]. HCNNG instead builds multiple hierarchical clusterings and merges them into a proximity graph, leveraging both global and local structure. By combining clustering with MST-based connectivity, HCNNG re- duces construction overhead while maintaining competitive query performance [49]. Some methods integrate hierarchical tree structures with graph refinement, while large-scale libraries such as FAISS [ 35] adopt hierarchical inverted file strategies. In FAISS, coarse quantization partitions the dataset into clusters, which are then refined with product quantization (PQ) [32].

Hierarchical Methods for ANN. A notable class of approaches for solving the ANN problem is based on hierarchical structures. One of the most widely used methods in this category is Hierarchical Navigable Small World ( HNSW ) [46], which constructs a multi- layered structure of navigable small-world graphs to enable efficient search. Interestingly, the core idea of hierarchical organization can be traced back to earlier work in computational geometry, including Cover Trees [6] and Navigating Nets [36]. Hierarchical Navigable Small World (HNSW) graphs [ 46] con- struct a multi-layered hierarchy of navigable small world (NSW) graphs. An NSW graph serves as an efficient approximation of the Delaunay graph [ 25], which is known to be an optimal structure for solving the approximate nearest neighbor (ANN) problem [ 47]. The Delaunay graph is closely related to the Voronoi diagram, which partitions the space into cells based on their proximity to the points in the dataset. Unlike the Delaunay graph, which requires explicit geometric computation, NSW graphs are built incrementally by inserting points and connecting them to their approximate nearest neighbors [ 47]. During insertion and querying, HNSW employs a greedy search algorithm (Algorithm 1) to navigate through the graph and locate nearby points. To improve scalability, HNSW orga- nizes the data in a hierarchy where the number of nodes decreases exponentially across layers, resulting in 𝑂(log𝑛)layers and a total space complexity of 𝑂(𝑛). The Cover Tree [ 6] and Navigating Nets [ 36] are hierarchical data structures for nearest neighbor search in general metric spaces. Both achieve logarithmic query times by recursively organizing data into nested layers, cover trees through covering and separa- tion invariants, and navigating nets via sequences of 𝑟-nets that approximate the dataset at multiple scales. While they offer strong theoretical guarantees and predictable performance, these methods are challenging to implement and scale poorly in practice, limiting their adoption in modern large-scale applications. Beyond HNSW, several other hierarchical indices and heuris- tics have been proposed. None being generalized to HENN. For example, HVS organizes data into coarse Voronoi regions that are refined hierarchically, enabling layered navigation and accelerating search by progressively narrowing the candidate set [ 43]. HCNNG instead builds multiple hierarchical clusterings and merges them into a proximity graph, leveraging both global and local structure. By combining clustering with MST-based connectivity, HCNNG re- duces construction overhead while maintaining competitive query performance [49]. Some methods integrate hierarchical tree structures with graph refinement, while large-scale libraries such as FAISS [ 35] adopt hierarchical inverted file strategies. In FAISS, coarse quantization partitions the dataset into clusters, which are then refined with product quantization (PQ) [32].

Other Solutions for ANN. Solutions to the nearest neighbor prob- lem can be categorized along several dimensions. One common dis- tinction is between classical methods, which primarily target the ex- act NN problem. Examples include k-d trees [ 5], ball trees [ 53], and Delaunay triangulations [ 26]. While effective in low-dimensional spaces, these methods typically fail to scale in high-dimensional settings. Another broad category includes quantization-based meth- ods [ 21,32,54], which cluster the data and represent points by theirassigned centroids (codewords), thereby approximating distances efficiently. Additionally, hashing-based methods such as Locality- Sensitive Hashing (LSH [ 11]) provide theoretical guarantees and have been widely used for high-dimensional ANN, and finally, the graph-based methods [ 43,46,47,58]. For comprehensive overviews of these and other approaches, we refer the reader to the following surveys [ 4,24,40,42,55,63]. Beyond graph topology, several lines of work improve ANN accuracy and efficiency through quantiza- tion. Guo, et al. [ 23] introduce direction-sensitive quantizers that better preserve angular similarity, enabling faster high-dimensional inference with competitive recall. Similarly, Rabitq [ 20] provides a quantization scheme with theoretical reconstruction-error guar- antees designed specifically for ANN search, showing that quanti- zation can substantially reduce memory while retaining accuracy. These works mainly focus on compressing the data vectors used for distance estimation, whereas our focus is on the structure and navigability of the search graph itself. Another complementary line is probabilistic search guidance [ 44], which proposes stochastic transition rules to escape local minima and improve robustness of greedy search. Such methods modify the search dynamics rather than the graph structure. The above systems are orthogonal and compatible with our theoretical contributions. Quantization-based methods can be applied inside any graph index to reduce vector memory footprint. Similarly, probabilistic routing modifies how the search moves on a fixed graph.

Similarly, Rabitq [ 20] provides a quantization scheme with theoretical reconstruction-error guar- antees designed specifically for ANN search, showing that quanti- zation can substantially reduce memory while retaining accuracy. These works mainly focus on compressing the data vectors used for distance estimation, whereas our focus is on the structure and navigability of the search graph itself. Another complementary line is probabilistic search guidance [ 44], which proposes stochastic transition rules to escape local minima and improve robustness of greedy search. Such methods modify the search dynamics rather than the graph structure. The above systems are orthogonal and compatible with our theoretical contributions. Quantization-based methods can be applied inside any graph index to reduce vector memory footprint. Similarly, probabilistic routing modifies how the search moves on a fixed graph.

Other Solutions for ANN. Solutions to the nearest neighbor prob- lem can be categorized along several dimensions. One common dis- tinction is between classical methods, which primarily target the ex- act NN problem. Examples include k-d trees [ 5], ball trees [ 53], and Delaunay triangulations [ 26]. While effective in low-dimensional spaces, these methods typically fail to scale in high-dimensional settings. Another broad category includes quantization-based meth- ods [ 21,32,54], which cluster the data and represent points by theirassigned centroids (codewords), thereby approximating distances efficiently. Additionally, hashing-based methods such as Locality- Sensitive Hashing (LSH [ 11]) provide theoretical guarantees and have been widely used for high-dimensional ANN, and finally, the graph-based methods [ 43,46,47,58]. Worst-Case Performance Analysis. Several works study the lim- itations of graph-based ANN indices. Indyk et al. [ 30] show that HNSW can require linear query time on adversarial datasets. Wang et al. [ 64] propose Steiner-hardness as a graph-native measure of query difficulty, capturing structural factors that influence cost and enabling the design of unbiased workloads. While these ap- proaches characterize hard queries or highlight specific failure cases on proximity graphs , our analysis takes a complementary view by providing general bounds on query time for HENN as a function of the underlying proximity graph. Moreover, empirical results sug- gest that the worst-case recall bounds rarely manifest in practice, as they remain stable across real-world datasets.

Comparison with Other Structural Analysis. Other recent works focus on improving or analyzing proximity graph constructions. Yang et al. [ 66] revisit construction strategies for indices like RNG and NSWG, optimizing pruning and edge selection to reduce build time without harming query performance. Diwan et al. [ 14] study the fundamental limits of navigable graphs, proving upper and lower bounds on node degree for efficient greedy routing. In con- trast, our contribution is structural: we introduce HENN as a graph- agnostic framework based on 𝜀-net layering, yielding provable polylogarithmic query-time guarantees for any underlying prox- imity graph. DiskANN [ 31] shows that a navigable graph com- bined with SSD-aware prefetching enables billion-scale search with near–HNSW accuracy. Lin & Zhao [ 41] provide a critical examina- tion of proximity-graph search, showing that well-constructed flat graphs can perform competitively and highlighting when greedy search succeeds or fails. Practical engineering optimizations also matter: Coleman et al. [ 10] demonstrate that simple node reordering can substantially reduce cache misses and latency. Most recently, Munyampirwa et al. [ 50] show that the performance of HNSW largely comes from a set of high-degree “hub” nodes, and that flattening the hierarchy yields similar recall and speed.
